analysis.one_liner: Gives digital money-transfer companies access to the Fed's instant payment system to cut remittance fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the last week before the session ended and died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Remittance Act would require the Federal Reserve to let affordable digital remittance providers — companies that help immigrants send money to family abroad — connect directly to FedNow, the Fed's instant payment network that is currently open only to banks. The bill says cheaper payment rails could push the cost of sending money home down from about 6% toward the World Bank's 3% target. It would also require the Fed to report to Congress each year on remittance cost trends.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrant workers and their families, who currently pay some of the highest fees of any consumer financial product — about 6% on average on the roughly $860 billion sent home globally each year. If digital remittance providers can settle payments instantly through FedNow rather than through bank intermediaries, the bill's findings argue those savings could be passed to senders as lower fees and faster delivery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants sending money home to family

how_it_helps.text: Remittance fees average about 6% globally and remittances total roughly $860 billion a year, making them the largest source of financial support to emerging markets; any cut in fees is direct money back into working families' pockets.

FedNow access could let digital remittance providers settle payments instantly and cheaply instead of routing through correspondent banks, which the bill's findings say could further drive down costs from the current ~6% toward the World Bank's 3% goal.

The bill includes guardrails: eligible providers must be registered with FinCEN or comply with the Bank Secrecy Act, be regulated by a state or federal consumer-protection agency, and be primarily in the remittance business — banks are explicitly excluded from the benefit.
The Fed could not impose capital or liquidity requirements on eligible providers beyond what is needed to make sure payments complete, keeping the compliance burden light for small fintech firms.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and the incumbent payment intermediaries who collect fees for moving remittance money. Today they sit between senders and recipients and earn a share of the ~6% average cost; direct FedNow access would let non-bank competitors bypass much of that fee stream. Traditional money-transfer companies like Western Union could also face cheaper digital competition.

drawbacks.text: Opening FedNow to non-bank fintechs raises financial-integrity and safety questions: the bill explicitly bars the Fed from imposing capital or liquidity requirements on these providers except to ensure payments complete, so if a provider fails mid-transfer, consumers could have little recourse.
The Fed would have to define "affordable remittance provider" with few hard criteria — it must exclude banks but otherwise has latitude — leaving room for judgment calls about which firms qualify.

Direct FedNow access does not automatically lower prices; providers could keep the savings as margin rather than passing them to senders, though the required annual report on remittance costs would give Congress visibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real and specific: remittance fees are among the most regressive charges in consumer finance, hitting low-wage workers hardest, and settlement infrastructure is a plausible lever to cut them. The main downside is prudential — extending the Fed's instant-payment rails to lightly regulated non-banks could concentrate settlement risk in firms with no capital requirements. The bill attempts to manage this with BSA registration and consumer-protection oversight requirements, but critics could fairly call the safety framework thinner than the one banks operate under.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Financial Services Committee in the closing weeks of the session, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres introduced the bill on October 25, 2024 — about ten weeks before the 118th Congress expired.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day, and the committee took no further action on it.
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and incumbent payment intermediaries keep their exclusive access to the Fed's instant-payment rails and the fee income from routing remittances. Immigrant families continue paying roughly 6% on the money they send home.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Remittance Act to open FedNow to affordable remittance providers.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, took no action to advance the bill before his chairmanship ended with the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of where members stood beyond the Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Banks currently have exclusive access to FedNow and earn fees handling remittance flows through correspondent relationships. The bill excludes banks from the new access and would let non-bank competitors settle directly, trimming the intermediaries' fee stream — though their current position persists because the bill died.

The bill hands these firms direct access to the Fed's instant payment rails, which their business model is built to monetize through lower fees and faster transfers. Their interest runs alongside senders' because both benefit when transfer costs fall.

industries.industry: Traditional money-transfer companies (e.g. Western Union-style operators)
industries.note: These incumbents collect a share of the ~6% average remittance cost. Direct FedNow settlement would make their fee-heavy networks easier to undercut with near-instant, cheaper digital transfers.
